statements.quote: But I very much think it will. When we cheer for murder, we get more murder.
statements.context: New intro (2024-12-07) after the CEO of UnitedHealthcare was murdered in New York and the public celebrated. The author argues that lionizing the killer in the press and on social media rewards the behavior ('when you pay attention to behavior, you get more of it') and predicts the violence will spread: 'Maybe we can imagine that's not going to spread? But I very much think it will.'
statements.confidence_phrase: I very much think it will
statements.note: Sincere prediction in the fresh intro to a republished satire piece; predicts more copycat violence.

statements.quote: the person killed will now never be a witness for the government in prosecution against others at his company for insider trading
statements.context: Same intro. Aside inside the author's argument against cheering the murder; it presupposes a government prosecution of other UnitedHealth Group executives for insider trading (which the author has alleged in earlier posts) in which the dead CEO can no longer testify.
statements.note: Near-truism (a dead person cannot testify); the forward-looking content is the presupposed insider-trading prosecution of UHG executives. Borderline.

statements.quote: This way, many many more treatments will not meet criteria for approval, without the manual labor of having to do peer-to-peer reviews
statements.context: Republished satirical open letter, section 'Abandoning My Life's Best Work Gem #1: More Robust Prior Auths!'. The author's mock proposal that Optum Insights build natural language processing software that reads prior records to stop clinicians from fitting diagnoses to prior-authorization criteria; he says many more treatments would then fail approval.
statements.note: Satirical proposal, conditional on a mock system being adopted. Logged for recall; the author labels the whole piece satire.

statements.quote: If we keep tinkering with numbers, everyone will start gaming things out in ever more economically productive ways… for UnitedHealth Group of course!
statements.context: Republished satirical open letter, 'Gem #2: Our New Approve a Claim, Deny a Claim Program!'. Mock program conscripting every in-network physician as a claims reviewer with incentives to deny colleagues' requests; the author says the incentives would make everyone game the system for UnitedHealth Group's benefit. He adds that the current unpaid fight against denials 'is not actually more crazy'.
statements.note: Satire; conditional on a mock program. The author partly endorses the underlying point about denial incentives.

statements.quote: All of the above could be litigated, and even lose billions.
statements.context: Republished open letter, 'Gem #3: Rage in Favor of the Machine and Its Subsidiaries!', framed as sincere analysis ('Here is how insane their incentives are'). Bulleted list: UnitedHealth Group's system of collecting disability disclosures before rejecting applicants invites class-action litigation in New York, plus retaliation in hiring; the author says these could be litigated and UHG could lose billions.
statements.note: Hedged litigation-risk call inside a satirical piece; this section reads as sincere. Compound (class action + retaliation).

statements.quote: And those expenses, all of those expenses , would find their way to the UnitedHealth Group balance sheet in a way that increased the total cost of doing business for their health insurance business, and thus increased the amount of profits they were allowed to make using a fixed medical loss ratio calculation .
statements.context: Immediately follows the 'could be litigated, and even lose billions' bullet. Conditional claim: litigation losses would raise UnitedHealth Group's cost base and, under the fixed medical loss ratio rule, raise the profit it is allowed to make ('UnitedHealth Group = More Profits From More Expenses'; footnote 35: 'getting sued drives up costs... that's how United becomes more profitable').
statements.note: Conditional on the prior litigation call; mechanism claim about the medical loss ratio. Compound.

statements.quote: That young man is now a friend, and he’s also going to train in child and adolescent psychiatry.
statements.context: Footnote 16 of the republished letter, on the author's public disclosure of his own bipolar disorder inspiring a hopeless medical student who heard him on Clubhouse; the author says this student is going to train in child and adolescent psychiatry.
statements.note: Personal statement about an unnamed third party's career plan; low forecast value.

statements.quote: turn that approach into a patentable technology which is now being brought to market by Magnus Medical
statements.context: Footnote 18 on the author's paper on rapid remission of suicidal depression with brain stimulation. He says Nolan Williams's Stanford lab standardized the protocol (SNT), completed randomized controlled trial work, and that the patented technology is being brought to market by Magnus Medical.
statements.confidence_phrase: is now being brought to market
statements.note: Present-progressive statement that implies future commercial availability of SNT. Borderline forward-looking; text is a republished older piece.

statements.quote: I would invite you to the live class today on working as an out-of-network provider, but it sold out last night, so you'll have to wait for the next one.
statements.context: Author's intro before the guest essay by Ben Spielberg. The author's live class on working as an out-of-network provider sold out; he says there will be a next one.
statements.note: Own-newsletter programming promise; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Johnson & Johnson’s branded esketamine (note the prefix es ) is on track to reach coveted “blockbuster status.”
statements.context: Guest essay by Ben Spielberg (founder of Bespoke Treatment), narrated by the author, on why ketamine clinics keep closing. Section 'Spravato: Coming In Hot': J&J's esketamine (Spravato, FDA approved for MDD in 2019) is said to be on track for blockbuster status; he reports his clinic's ketamine infusion census fell over 70% as insured Spravato ($20 copay) took share.
statements.note: Guest author Ben Spielberg's claim; the author narrates it 'with only light edits' and neither adopts nor disputes it.

statements.quote: While many successful clinics exist today, the wheels tend to start to fall off when scaling, where all of a sudden, a clinic’s reach has surpassed its captive population. Otherwise, it becomes a series of continual cost-cutting until there is nothing left to cut… save for the business itself.
statements.context: Closing of the guest essay by Ben Spielberg. Generalization that cash-pay ketamine clinics fail when they scale past their local population or cost-cut until the business itself is cut; the essay's thesis (Numinus selling its clinics to Stella as the latest example) is that ketamine clinic chains keep closing or selling for pennies on the dollar.
statements.note: Guest author's habitual generalization that implies continued ketamine clinic failures. Borderline forward-looking.

statements.quote: Thanks for listening, and we will be back with more writing tomorrow.
statements.context: Short post pointing readers to the author's appearance on The Mental Health Forecast podcast by Arjun Nanda, M.D.; promises more newsletter writing the next day.
statements.note: Routine publishing promise; low forecast value. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: we are getting our first Trader Joe’s sometime soon
statements.context: Guest essay by Ben Greenzweig (Founder of Living Water Mental Health BRAIN Treatment Center) describing Horry County, South Carolina; local aside that the county has no Whole Foods but will get a Trader Joe's soon.
statements.note: Guest author's local aside with no psychiatric relevance; logged for completeness.

statements.quote: This year, I was blessed to preach twice at my church and have been asked to deliver messages again in 2025.
statements.context: Guest author Ben Greenzweig on his faith journey at Low Country Community Church in Murrells Inlet, SC; says he has been asked to preach again in 2025.
statements.note: Guest author's personal plan; low forecast value.

statements.quote: He quickly replied, “ There’s no reason ,” and that’s when the idea for Living Water Mental Health BRAIN Treatment Center was hatched.
statements.context: Guest author Ben Greenzweig recounts asking the author (early 2024) whether Fermata-style drug-free neuromodulation (TMS with reported 79% remission and relief in as little as 5 days) could exist in Horry County or only in big cities like New York. The author answered there is no reason it cannot, i.e. the model can succeed in a rural/semi-rural market.
entities: Living Water Mental Health BRAIN Treatment Center
statements.note: The author's stance as quoted by the guest author; the author edits and publishes it without dissent and is Medical Director of the clinic. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: he shared that he was in the process of building another company with two healthcare veterans, called Breakthrough6 , that would be in the business of planting hundreds of mental health treatment centers throughout the country.
statements.context: Guest author Ben Greenzweig reports the author's plan for Breakthrough6 (with healthcare veterans Robert Jordshaugen and Lincoln Fish): a company to plant hundreds of mental health treatment centers across the US, providing clinical infrastructure to scale rapidly with non-invasive neuromodulation prescribed virtually by a physician but administered locally. Living Water (opened November 2024) is its pilot site.
entities: Living Water Mental Health BRAIN Treatment Center
statements.note: Author's own-company plan (Breakthrough6) as reported by the guest author; numeric ('hundreds of' centers). Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: a very generous financial hardship scholarship program that would provide over an 80% reduction in treatment cost to the most financially disadvantaged people
statements.context: Guest author Ben Greenzweig describes the practice plan that Living Water and Breakthrough6 (the author is Medical Director of Living Water) developed for Horry County: revenue from some government and private insurance, self-pay, and a hardship scholarship cutting treatment cost by over 80% for the poorest patients.
entities: Living Water Mental Health BRAIN Treatment Center
statements.note: Guest author's plan statement with a numeric target (over 80% cost reduction); the author is Medical Director of the clinic. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: My goal is that as new FDA-cleared modalities become available, we can reduce the dual stigma surrounding mental health
statements.context: Guest author Ben Greenzweig's aim for Living Water: a community-driven infrastructure that embraces novel breakthrough mental health treatments; the sentence presupposes that new FDA-cleared modalities will become available.
entities: Living Water Mental Health BRAIN Treatment Center
statements.note: Goal statement; the forward-looking content is only the embedded expectation of new FDA-cleared modalities. Borderline.

statements.quote: This approach is about as grassroots as it gets, but I believe the investment will be worth it.
statements.context: Guest author Ben Greenzweig on his outreach for Living Water (farmers' markets and fairs, the Carolina AM morning show, a men's group, preaching, a pastors' breakfast, veterans' organizations); he expects the grassroots investment to pay off.
entities: Living Water Mental Health BRAIN Treatment Center
statements.note: Guest author's expectation about his own nonprofit's outreach.

statements.quote: I don't know if all our patients will respond positively to treatment. Statistically, some may not.
statements.context: Guest author Ben Greenzweig writing in early December 2024, after Living Water's first patient (intake HAM-D 27) reached HAM-D 0 after several days of TMS. He notes uncertainty about working capital for the self-funded nonprofit and expects that statistically some future patients will not respond.
entities: Living Water Mental Health BRAIN Treatment Center
statements.note: Hedged expectation about future patient outcomes at the clinic where the author is Medical Director.

statements.quote: It might even make it to a patient sooner rather than later.
statements.context: Author's opening on the 17-year average lag from scientific publication to clinical practice. He explains research to readers so they can apply it for themselves, family, practice or friends, with the hedged expectation that the research (here accelerated and deep TMS) reaches patients faster.
statements.note: Vague, hedged; the antecedent of 'it' is research reaching clinical practice via informed readers.

statements.quote: There's more coming every day and more hope — we're trying to make it more accessible, too.
statements.context: Closing of a post on Brainsway's published pilot of accelerated deep TMS (H7 coil) in alcohol use disorder in veterans and the author's Fermata case series with Irfan Handoo (dTMS with H1/H7 coils, 69.05% mean remission in six patients refractory to rTMS, ECT and IV ketamine). The author says more such data is coming and his shop is working to make the treatment more accessible.
statements.note: Vague forward-looking promise about upcoming data and accessibility; own-organization (Fermata). Coder may mark CONTROL.
